{{short description|American biologist}}
'''Sarah P. Gibbs'''  (May 25, 1930 – September 25, 2014)<ref name="obituary" /> was Emeritus Professor of Biology at [[McGill University]] in Canada, where she was initially appointed as an assistant professor on tenure track in September 1966.<ref name="agendas" /> She was a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Canada]], and a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and she received the 2003 Gilbert Morgan Smith medal for research on algae.<ref name="ARAutobiography" />

Gibbs was born on May 25, 1930, in Boston, and  received a bachelor's degree  in zoology in 1952 at  [[Cornell University]] in Ithaca, New York.<ref name="ARAutobiography">{{cite journal |author=Gibbs, Sarah P.|title=Looking at Life: From Binoculars to the Electron Microscope |journal=Annual Review of Plant Biology |volume=57 |pages=1–17 |year=2006 |pmid=16669753 |doi=10.1146/annurev.arplant.57.032905.105413 |doi-access=free }}</ref> She  continued at Cornell completing  a Master's program  in zoology with a minor in education. Her first scientific position, post-Master's degree, was working as a technician for zoology professor Marcus Singer.<ref name="ARAutobiography"/>
She moved with her then-husband, Bob Gibbs, to [[Woods Hole, Massachusetts]],  and  obtained a part-time laboratory technician position with [[Ralph Lewin]] at the [[Marine Biological Laboratory]] (MBL) where [[Albert Szent-Györgyi]] had a laboratory. In Lewin's laboratory, she was able to run her own experiments. While still a technician, Gibbs applied to study in the lab of [[Kenneth Thimann]] at [[Harvard University]] as a PhD student. She started working toward a PhD  at Harvard in the fall of 1958 as a National Science Foundation Fellow, graduating with a PhD degree in November 1961.<ref name="agendas">{{cite book |author=Gibbs, Sarah P. |year=1995 |title=Our Own Agendas: Autobiographical Essays by Women Associated with McGill University |publisher=McGill-Queen's Press |pages=47–59}}</ref>

While at Harvard, Gibbs switched advisors, completing her PhD under the advisement of George Chapman, studying  the [[pyrenoid]] structure in algae, as well as the ultrastructure of the [[chloroplast]] itself. In 1962, she published a paper titled "Nuclear envelope-chloroplast relationships in algae",<ref name="envelope">{{cite journal |author=Gibbs, Sarah P.|title=Nuclear envelope-chloroplast relationships in algae |journal=Journal of Cell Biology |volume=14 |pages=433–444 |year=1962 |pmid=13947685  |url=http://jcb.rupress.org/content/14/3/433.full.pdf |doi=10.1083/jcb.14.3.433 |pmc=2106112 |issue=3}}</ref> detailing the unexpected discovery that in a number of algal classes the chloroplasts are surrounded by four, not two, membranes. Gibbs called the two extra membranes the outer envelope, but they were later named the chloroplast [[endoplasmic reticulum]] (ER) in a paper published by Ben Bouck in 1965.<ref name="ARAutobiography" />

She died in Newport, New Hampshire, at the age of 84.<ref name="obituary">{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |title=Sarah Preble Gibbs |url=http://montrealgazette.remembering.ca/obituary/sarah-gibbs-1930-2014-1066193987 |work=Montreal Gazette |location=Montreal |date=2014-10-04 |access-date=2019-03-03 }}</ref>
